titleText.es: La única sangre con la que se van a firmar estos contratos es con la que me salga al cortarme intentando abrir la maldita caja del CD.
titleText.en: The only blood these contracts are signed in is from me cutting my hand trying to open the goddamn CD case.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive localizes Faust as Fausto and closely translates the official title text's blood-contract and difficult-CD-case joke. No source metadata anomaly was found.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the familiar listener as the recipient and sits before traigo, the verb changed for the speaker.
Lee is leer's positive command for one familiar listener.

regions.labelEs: "AL ENTRAR EN ESTA HABITACIÓN ACEPTA PERDER SU PROPIA ALMA EN VEZ DE NEGOCIAR CON EL MORTAL QUE EN ELLA RESIDE...

applications.explanationEn: Al introduces the time relationship, and entrar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Acepta is the formal singular form that states agreement, and perder supplies the accepted action in its unchanged dictionary form.
En vez de introduces the alternative, and negociar supplies that alternative as an unchanged action verb.
Que links mortal to the added identifying information; en ella supplies the place and reside supplies the action.
Espera is esperar's positive command for one familiar listener.

regions.labelEs: MEFISTÓFELES SE ENCUENTRA CON LA E.U.L.A.

excludedUnits.rationale: E.U.L.A. is the English abbreviation for End User License Agreement, retained as the joke's software term rather than Spanish vocabulary. Vision emitted four duplicate full-acronym boxes, one for each letter.

applications.explanationEn: Se and encuentra form the singular meeting expression, con introduces what is encountered, and la begins the filled object; the English acronym remains visible but unscheduled.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, mortal means a human being viewed as someone who will eventually die. It can appear with an article, as in el mortal, or as a direct form of address without one.

example.es: Los mortales no viven para siempre.
example.en: Mortals do not live forever.

cards.answerEn: to you; for you (one familiar person)
cards.noteEn: Te can identify one familiar listener as the person who receives something or benefits from an action. It normally comes before a verb that has changed for the person and time.

example.en: I am bringing you a coffee.

cards.promptEs: me/te/le/nos/os/les delante del verbo que cambia
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the short word that identifies who receives something?
cards.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before the first verb that changes for the person and time.
cards.noteEn: The slashes in the prompt mean to choose the one receiver word that fits. A verb that changes for the person and time is often called a conjugated verb: estoy rather than the dictionary form estar. In a multiword verb phrase, the receiver word goes before that changed verb, so les estoy enviando places les before estoy, not between estoy and enviando.

example.en: I am sending them a photo.

cards.noteEn: Traigo is the present form of traer used when the speaker says yo. The middle of the verb changes: traer becomes traigo.

example.en: I am bringing bread for dinner.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Lee is the positive command from leer used when telling one familiar person to read.

example.en: Read this message.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.answerEn: Use al followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Al + verb tells when the main action happens. Translate it naturally as “when,” “on,” or “upon”: al llegar means “when arriving” or simply “when someone arrives.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say “when doing something” or “upon doing something”?

example.en: When I arrive, I will call you.

cards.noteEn: Acepta is the present form of aceptar used for usted, the polite or formal way to address one person. The same written form can also mean “he accepts” or “she accepts.”

example.en: You agree to the conditions.

cards.promptEs: aceptar + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone accepts or agrees to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of aceptar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign in the prompt shows the order of the two pieces. The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Aceptar changes for the person and time, while the action verb stays unchanged: acepto ayudar, acepta esperar, aceptaron pagar. Do not insert a or de between them.

example.en: Lucía agrees to help.

cards.noteEn: With formal usted, su can mean “your.” The same form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their,” so context identifies the owner.

example.en: Ma’am, here is your coffee.

cards.noteEn: Propia emphasizes that something belongs to the person already identified. It takes the feminine singular form when it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.en: Clara made her own decision.

cards.questionEn: What makes the soul-bargain scene a parody of a software agreement?
cards.answerEn: Mephistopheles traditionally bargains for Faust's soul; the comic makes him lose that leverage to an end-user software license agreement.
cards.noteEn: In the Faust legend, Mephistopheles offers knowledge or power in exchange for Faust's soul. E.U.L.A. is the English abbreviation for End User License Agreement, the terms a software user accepts. The sign turns those routine terms into a prior contract that blocks the demon's negotiation.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: En belongs to the fixed three-word connector en vez de. Learn the connector as a unit rather than translating en as ordinary ‘in.’

example.es: Tomé té en vez de café.
example.en: I had tea instead of coffee.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one option replaces another?
cards.answerEn: Put en vez de before the alternative that was not chosen: ‘instead of.’
cards.noteEn: A noun, pronoun, or unchanged action verb can follow: en vez de café, en vez de eso, en vez de llamar. The three words en vez de stay together.

example.es: Usamos el tren en vez del coche.
example.en: We used the train instead of the car.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; forms en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: Vez often means an occurrence or time, but inside en vez de it helps form the fixed connector ‘instead of.’

example.es: Fuimos andando en vez de tomar el autobús.
example.en: We walked instead of taking the bus.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: De finishes the connector en vez de and comes directly before the alternative that is not chosen.

example.es: Escribió un correo en vez de llamar.
example.en: She wrote an email instead of calling.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: it (referring to a feminine thing after a preposition)
cards.noteEn: After a preposition such as en, con, or de, ella can refer back to a feminine singular thing as well as to a woman. English normally uses “it” for the thing.

example.es: La caja está vacía; no hay nada en ella.
example.en: The box is empty; there is nothing in it.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to
no separate English word; helps encontrarse con mean ‘to meet’ or ‘encounter’
cards.noteEn: Encontrarse uses a short matching word such as me, te, se, nos, or os. Se is the form used with one third-person subject such as Ana or Mefistófeles.

example.es: Ana se encuentra con un vecino.
example.en: Ana runs into a neighbor.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone meets, encounters, or runs into a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of encontrarse, then con and the person or thing encountered.
cards.noteEn: Encontrarse includes a short word that matches the person doing the meeting: me encuentro, te encuentras, se encuentra, nos encontramos, or se encuentran. Con stays before the person or thing encountered. This differs from encontrarse en, which describes where something is located, and from encontrar without the matching short word, which commonly means “to find.”

example.es: Marta se encuentra con un amigo.
example.en: Marta runs into a friend.

cards.noteEn: Encuentra is the present form used for one third-person subject. With se before it and con after it, se encuentra con describes meeting or coming across someone or something.

example.en: Leo meets Marta.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; required before who or what is encountered
cards.noteEn: Spanish keeps con in encontrarse con alguien or algo. Natural English normally says “meet someone” or “encounter something” without a separate word for con.

example.en: I ran into Julia.
